notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0057.tlg047.1st1K-gr: 1.1: 'ἐνίων δὲ εἰς ἀρχὴν ὀλιγοχρόνιον εἰσάγειν τὴν ἀκμήν' is obscure; rendered literally ('bring the peak into a beginning of short duration'), the sense may be that some merge the peak into a brief opening phase. 'ἐξ ἀποκοπῆς' ('by cutting off') appears to be a technical term for abrupt resolution without decline. 2.1: the quotations are from the Hippocratic Aphorisms (II.29, II.30, I.22, I.24); 'ἢν μὴ ὀργᾷ' rendered 'unless they are in turgescence'. 3.1: 'πραγμα τείᾳ' read as πραγματείᾳ (scanning split); '(εἰ)' is an editorial supplement, translated.

In 5.1 'some of them have the constitution, when they have it precisely brought to completion' appears defective; a word such as 'fatal' (or a phrase) seems to have dropped out after 'constitution', marked [...]. The word for 'common' (καινός, 'new', as printed) is read as κοινός. In 4.1 'οὗ τος' is read as οὗτος, and '(ἔστιν)' is an editorial supplement left untranslated as redundant.

In 7.1 'τὸν ἀρχῆς' is read as 'τὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς'. In 6.1 'κριμνώδη' and 'πεταλώδη' (particles in urine) are rendered 'bran-like' and 'leaf-like'; the exact appearance meant is uncertain. 'ἀγωνιστικόν' (treatment) rendered 'vigorous' (i.e. active, combative).

nodes.text: GALEN'S BOOK ON THE STAGES OF THE DISEASE AS A WHOLE.

Well then, we conceive of stages of the disease as a whole analogous to the ages of living creatures: one, the first, that of its coming into being; the second, that of its ascent; the third, that of its peak; and the fourth, that of its decline, at least when the patients are going to be saved. For if they die before that, either during the ascent or at the peak, it is quite clear that such a disease has not gone through all the stages. But even the disease that does go through them is open to dispute about almost all of its parts. Some say that the peak is a single moment, grasped by thought alone. Some say that in certain cases, as in the continuous [fevers], there is no peak at all. Some bring the peak into a beginning of short duration. Others remove the beginning, not only in these but in all other diseases as well. Others again sometimes remove the decline too, if the disease is resolved 'by cutting off', as they call it. First, then, we must settle these disputes; next, articulate precisely the concepts of the stages of the disease as a whole; after that, state their distinguishing signs; and then, in order, it would be time to show their usefulness, combining [them] with what concerns the periods.

Now the beginning of the disease, in so far as it sets in at some moment when the healthy condition collapses, is in all diseases conceived of as having no extension in time. Along with this, however, it is not granted that every disease has something like a coming into being, such as we conceive of in living creatures. For diseases are not composed of certain parts, as a living creature is composed of head, chest and limbs. For when they fall away from the natural state, they come into being in a brief instant of time, and from then on they ascend up to the peak. For let the disease, say, be one of bad mixture, the kind by which, as I have shown, fever too is constituted. It is necessary, then, that as soon as this unnatural heat first arises, the person has a fever, and that the heat intensifies up to the peak. For how could there be a coming into being in time of something that has no parts? I said this at the very beginning as well, and I answered it by recalling the fevers that set in with chilling. In the case of the periods that answer is sufficient: for the stage of chilling is one of the particular stages, and the first in order, of the whole disease. But it would be utterly ridiculous to consider the first stage of the first paroxysm the beginning of the whole disease. For this stage, which they call the beginning of the disease, has its usefulness with regard to remedies, and it was with an eye to it that [Hippocrates] said: 'When diseases are beginning, if anything seems [to need] moving, move [it]; but when they are at their peak, it is better to keep quiet.' Likewise he also said this: 'Around the beginnings and the ends all things are weaker.' And further there is what was said about purging, that one should purge and move [humours] when they are concocted, not when raw, nor at the beginnings, unless they are in turgescence. And in addition to these, there is: 'In acute affections use purgatives rarely and at the beginnings.' And many other things besides these, said partly by Hippocrates and partly by all the other ancient physicians, do not allow us to take the beginning to be the onset of the first paroxysm, but [to extend it] over a longer span, so that one can let blood, and use an enema, and sometimes, if it is urgent, also purge; besides which it would be ridiculous to assign an equal beginning to diseases resolved within the seventh day and to those that persist for a year, as the quartan sometimes does. I have said much about this beginning also in the first [book] On Crises, showing how one might recognise this first stage. Its chief mark was the lack of concoction in the disease. But it is better here too to add to what was said there whatever is useful for the present discussion.

Let it be supposed, then, first, that the beginning of an inflammation is being sought. Who would not say that its quasi-coming-into-being lies in that whole period during which the part is being filled with bloody substance? For whether this happens through infiltration, or through the wedging of all the vessels, or through some obstruction caused by masses in the passages, or whether, as we have taught both in the treatise On Uneven Bad Mixture and in the one On Swellings Contrary to Nature, a certain excess of blood gathers in the part as the inflammation is generated, this will be the first stage, in which the part is being filled up, corresponding to the size of the affection. When the inflow stops, and what is contained in the inflamed part begins to putrefy, a certain heat arises through the putrefaction, and further diffusion through the heat, upon which pneuma too is generated, and through both of these the part is distended more than before, even if nothing more flows in: this is the second period, that of the growth of the inflammation. When it is now changing into pus, the greatest pains, no doubt, seize [the patient] at that time. For pains and fevers occur around the formation of the pus more than once it has formed; and such a stage is called the peak of the affection. If the flux, by suppurating or being dispersed, makes the swelling and the tension smaller, that is the beginning of the decline. That is how the stages are divided in inflammation. In fever, for the kind that arises upon an inflammation one should posit the same stages as for it; for the kind that arises from a humour without inflammation, [one should posit] the period of the non-concoction of the troublesome humours as the beginning; when they begin to be concocted, the beginning has ended and the second stage has come, called that of the ascent; when the concoction itself is most fully being accomplished, that of the peak; and next that of the decline, in which both the magnitude of the symptoms and the quantity of what is being concocted have now abated, and there is only a small remnant left of the humours that need to be concocted. In the treatise On Crises I also set out all the signs, both those of faint concoction and those of total non-concoction, and those of clear and of complete [concoction]: some proper to concoction in the stomach, some to that in the veins, and others again proper to the respiratory [organs]. They were taken partly from the excrements, partly from the urines, partly from the sputa. I went through these at very great length in that work together with the sayings of Hippocrates; in the present one it is enough to say only this much: that ulcers too have the same stages. For first watery, unconcocted and thin serous fluids flow from them; then next, less of them and thicker; and then thin pus; then this becomes less in quantity, but thicker and whiter. So there is none of the affections that are resolved which does not go through the stages. Nor is knowledge of them [obtained] from anything other than the signs of non-concoction and concoction, which are recognised through the residues. For who does not know that the stomach has failed to concoct, when he sees undigested excrements? And who does not know, on seeing watery urine, that concoction in the vessels has failed? And who, having seen thin sputum being coughed up in pleurisy or pneumonia, will not likewise understand that the affection is still at its beginning? So too in ophthalmias, at the beginning a great deal of thin, quite unconcocted [fluid] flows off; next, less and thicker, taking on some outline of concoction; then as time goes on, as the quantity diminishes and the consistency moves towards greater thickness, the [signs] of concoction increase so much that the eyelids of those who have slept are glued together by the rheum that forms, which itself is at first thin and abundant, but in time becomes less and thicker, and so indicates both the concoction of the disease and its decline. And again, in the [fluxes] that run down from the brain through the palate and nostrils, it is the beginning when what is carried down is watery and thin, abundant and acrid; for these indicate extreme non-concoction. Signs of concoction are, by now, that it is thicker, less acrid, and evacuated in small amount; and if what is called mucus and phlegm also comes away with it, this is already a surer sign of concoction; just as, if it becomes thicker than that and less, it indicates concoction much more still. These, then, are the stages of the diseases from which patients are saved.

About the other [stages], those in which patients perish, I shall speak a little later, after first articulating whatever in what has been said needs some distinction. One of these, then, is the question about the peak: whether it is always without duration, as far as it itself is concerned, even if to perception it often appears to stretch out over considerable spans of time; or whether it always has some breadth, sometimes greater, sometimes less; or whether in some diseases it has duration and in others none. Since the inquiry needs a longer discussion, I think I shall leave it aside altogether, imitating Hippocrates, who said about dislocation at the shoulder: 'I do not, however, insist on this, although I have something to say.' For just as he was content with what he had always seen, in the same way I too shall now speak as one who has always seen [it]. I have observed every peak of the individual paroxysms coming about over a span of time, so that even if by nature it were without duration, we would derive no use from that. For as soon as the decline becomes clear to perception, we then use the remedies suited to it; but as long as the magnitude of the fever stays at the same figures, so long is it fitting to do what is proper to the magnitude of the peak. In the same way, in ophthalmia and pleurisy and every inflammation, and in each of the other diseases, the general stages, measured by perception, dictate the use of the different remedies. The inquiry into the breadth of the peak, then, becomes a logical one, whether one is examining something about the individual paroxysms or about the disease as a whole; and at present it is not my purpose to make such distinctions, as those do who bring everything into everything, one of whom is Archigenes. For this man mixes into the most medical treatises sometimes an inquiry about names, and sometimes one about the things themselves, but a logical one. We, however, as we have always guarded against this, shall do so now too: leaving it to others to inquire about the peak, whether it is without duration or with some duration, we shall measure its usefulness, seeing nature plainly, both in the ages [of life], where the prime is spread over a broad span of time, and in diseases, sometimes over a longer [span], often over a shorter, but in any case over a perceptible one. This very difference in time is more plainly seen in the age of prime in animals; for indeed we see hunting dogs and racehorses already doing something of their proper work during the time of growth, and after that we say they have become mature, and we see plainly that they are stronger than before, and remain equally strong not for one year only, but sometimes for two and three years; just as human athletes too often remain of equal strength, as far as perception goes, not only for these three but for four and five years. So too, as I said, in diseases the individual paroxysms make their peaks over a clear span of time, and much more do the general stages of the disease as a whole have breadth, both all the others and no less that of the peak, as well as each of the rest. It is sometimes possible to recognise them clearly, sometimes only dimly, or even to be completely ignorant [of them] for a very long while. And for this reason some diseases seem to make their onset already at their peak. This in itself is one of the impossibilities; for not even the so-called continuous fever ever began straight from the peak, but from its first attack it reaches its most complete peak in four or three hours at the least, and from then on remains altogether equal to itself continuously until the crisis. But neither could one say that the disease which comes on most suddenly, apoplexy, is at its peak [from the start]; for that is not strictly so either: it passes through its beginning and ascent in a short time, but it is not without a beginning, nor does it come on straightaway in its most complete form, just as the epileptic paroxysm does not either. For no one is seized by the symptom as suddenly as those who have their neck cut off; and yet even their cutting has a first moment, a second, a third and a fourth, just as when a surgeon cuts anything at all. But, if you like, let it be granted that the epileptic and the apoplectic collapse occur without duration, so that I may go through what I proposed at the outset. For the collapse that occurs is itself a symptom, but the disease is not this; rather it must certainly be, as we have shown, some condition of the body. And if we have no sign of it either while it is coming into being or while it is increasing, this does not overturn the consistent argument by which we said that every disease must arrive at the peak through the ascent; rather it admits that the increase of diseases is sometimes hard to recognise, and in many cannot be recognised. That what I say is true I could persuade you by this very brief argument. I have often seen scirrhous swellings in the legs forming right from the beginning without any preceding inflammation, and growing little by little, sometimes for three or four years, without perceptibly hindering the necessary functions of the leg; but in time, because of their considerable size, later on they also troubled walking. Imagine, then, for it is not impossible, that some scirrhous swelling is already forming in the concave part of the liver; its formation will escape notice for a while, but later the [signs] of the condition itself will become more evident, though even then we cannot discover in what condition this occurs; and later in time a dropsical effusion will at some point also occur, while even then the scirrhous swelling gives no sign to the touch; but appearing later, of considerable size, it has reminded us of our earlier ignorance. Not a few, at any rate, have I seen who along such a course of symptoms revealed within a short time no small scirrhous swelling in the liver, which had been forming for a long while but escaped notice because of its smallness and the good nourishment of the muscles of the hypochondrium. But when the scirrhus, as it grows, both mounts onto the convex parts of the liver and becomes a cause of wasting both to the other parts of the animal and to the muscles of the hypochondrium, from both of these you will plainly recognise it in a short time, when it already has a considerable size. All such matters are bound up with the examination of the affected parts, which it is not our purpose to consider at present, but [these] have been pointed out, not uselessly, because of their connection. It is time to return to the original discussion. Each disease has its own time of coming into being, sometimes perceptible, sometimes not; after which again the time of increase is not equally perceptible in all, this one either; these are followed by that of the peak, which is always perceptible, while we admit that sometimes there is no plain sign of the beginning of the affection or of its increase. In these cases, then, with regard to the use of the art, one will truly say that only the stage of the peak exists; and if [the patients] are going to be saved, that the stage of decline always follows it, being perceptible and such as to occupy a span of time that is not without breadth. For even if someone has a sharp crisis through a haemorrhage or through sweats, there is at any rate some perceptible time of decline in this case too; and if in other diseases this is shorter, while elsewhere the decline lasts three or four or more days, this plainly does no harm to the earlier argument, nor does it discredit the main point of the statement, but it still stands: that all diseases which are resolved have, just as a peak, so also some decline.

With these things sufficiently demonstrated, we shall examine the diseases that are not resolved. Their nature is twofold: some of them have the constitution [...], when they have it precisely brought to completion; others are of the nature of those that are resolved, but when [the disease] kills first, it is in this respect that it happens to them [not to be resolved]. Of these too the manner is threefold: for it destroys before it is resolved either because of the patient's weakness, or because of the strength of the diseases, or because of both together. By another account there is one common pattern for all such [cases], when [the disease] is beyond the strength; for that which holds together the patient's death lies in this, since no one can be saved unless nature overcomes the disease, nor perish without nature being defeated and the disease becoming stronger than it. And for this reason some think that only one thing is signified by 'a great disease', [namely] what is constituted in relation to something, not knowing that 'great disease' is sometimes said in this way, as if we were saying 'greater', when it is beyond the strength; but it is also said according to its own substance, as a man or a horse or an ox [is called] great. I have demonstrated this double meaning many times already in other works; but to work out everything in every place is idle chatter. What is useful for the present, then, I shall state. Each disease possesses in and of itself a certain magnitude (for it is better to put it this way for clarity), and this magnitude of the disease is either beyond the strength, so as to weigh it down, or on the contrary weaker than the strength, so as to be overcome by it, provided everything is done well. When, then, it is beyond the strength, the person will certainly die.

The stages of the disease are then taken in one respect in the same way as those described earlier, but in another respect not in the same way. For the beginning has its constitution, in the same manner [as before], in the coming into being of the disease; but the ascent does not lie in [the disease] being concocted, as in those who are going to be saved, but in the signs of non-concoction and the deadly signs. For it was shown, if we remember at all, that these differ from one another, and for the sake of reminder some of them will be stated now too. The well-coloured urine, then, and moderately thick, is the best of all urines, as far as colour and consistency go; but there must certainly be present with it either a good suspension, or a cloud, or a sediment, as the nature of the disease requires; for we have shown that sediments arise in one way in bilious diseases, and in another in diseases from an abundance of raw humours. Diametrically opposed, as one might say, is the unconcocted urine, which has neither suspension nor sediment nor cloud, and has not even taken on any thickness or yellowness, but is white in colour and thin in consistency, like water; if, however, some black cloud or suspension, or a black sediment, appears in it, and still more if the whole is dark, it is deadly; just as also if certain bran-like or leaf-like [particles] appear in it; and indeed urine that smells strongly foul, and fatty urine, which they call oily, is deadly. These, then, are the urines that are signs of a great disease, which I said is great according to its own nature. And [the disease is] great also if the sputum in pleuritic and peripneumonic patients is either black, or strongly tawny, or frothy, or quite foul-smelling, or is not coughed up at all, while severe pain or difficulty of breathing grips the person. Analogous to these, in the other diseases too that arise in the liver or the stomach, there exists a class of deadly signs; hence it is not possible to define the peak in such diseases in the same way as the peak of those who will be saved. For there the greatest paroxysms marked off the peak, but here one cannot define the greatest ones in the same way, since the disease is not concocted at all; rather one must grasp in thought the greatest [magnitude] which the disease sometimes reaches, while at other times it kills first. In an inflammation that is being resolved, the formation of pus is the boundary of the peak; but in one that is not going to be resolved it is possible for the person to die even during its ascent; yet it is also possible for the strength, if it is very robust, to hold out until the final magnitude. For of this inflammation, when it is not going to be resolved, the greatest magnitude ends either in gangrene or in putrefaction; and until it is one of these, it can still increase. Let the increases in each class of the other diseases be understood analogously to inflammation. Not only their classes, but also their differences and species, have been stated in one treatise, which is entitled On the Differences of Diseases. But I ask you to pay attention above all to that point which, if overlooked, could seriously mislead someone.

For it is possible for a person to be held at one and the same time by two or even three diseases, of which one is already declining, another still remains in the stage of the beginning or the first part of the ascent, and another has increased to the utmost; and then the person dies, neither because of the declining one nor because of the one now beginning, but because of the one that has greatly increased. Above all, then, examine the three sources of the faculties that govern the whole body, how they are disposed: I mean the brain, the heart and the liver; and next all the other parts as well, those that grow from each of the sources, nerves, veins and arteries, and whatever parts have a nature of their own but are governed by all the sources, some equally, some more by one and less by another. For from such an examination you will find, first, whether there is one disease or several in the person; and then next examine the proper stages of each, which are necessary for finding the remedies, for the sake of which this discussion of ours is pursued.

For around the beginnings and the ends all things are weaker, around the peaks stronger, and in between these, those that are in between. For those nearer the beginning are weaker than those nearer the peak, as also are those nearer the end; and those equally distant from the beginning and the peak are midway in strength between both extremes; and likewise those equally distant from the peak and the end are also midway between their own extremes. In treatment, then, the soothing approach should prevail at the peak, and the vigorous approach at the beginning and the end; and let the intermediate stages be taken in proportion to the extremes, as has been said at greater length in the treatise On the Therapeutic Method; but now, by way of outline, I have gone through the main points themselves, showing the use of distinguishing the stages in diseases. For it is not possible to find out how one should regulate the diet, nor when one should feed, without determining them securely, if indeed one must infer right at the beginning when the peak of the disease will be, and how great the strength of the patient is. For if it will hold out through the stage of the peak even without taking food, it is best to fast until the decline has begun; but if it is not possible for the patient to hold out while fasting, he must be fed right from the beginning at every time that can admit food, and this is the time of remission. By remission I now mean the second part of the whole period, when it is divided into two parts in all, paroxysm and remission. Hippocrates, then, first of all those we know, made correct distinctions about this; but it would have been better to work out his art in detail; yet almost no one has done this, and some, departing from it completely, have turned aside into long-windedness, as Archigenes has, both in all his other works and in the two books he wrote on the stages in diseases. You will clearly learn what I mean by examining these two things precisely: first, whether what has now been said by us throughout this whole book is most useful for treatment and prognosis; and second, whether anything has been said by Archigenes. For if, while nothing is lacking in these [statements of ours], he is seen saying other things, he errs doubly, both not teaching what is useful and burdening the readers of his books with the verbosity of useless matter.
